extracted.intended_audience: public relations professionals, publicity counsel, and institutional leaders (universities, museums, social-service organizations, corporations)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for planning and executing propaganda/public-relations campaigns for institutions (universities, museums, social-service orgs, corporations), including media selection, event design, use of personalities, and ethical considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popularize technical messages
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical findings must be translated into language intelligible to the average man or woman; otherwise discoveries will remain unread outside technical publications (e.g., 'If left to his own devices, he might never have appeared in print...no more intelligible to the average man or woman than if they had been inscribed in Mayan hieroglyphics').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use press agents or publicity specialists to convert specialized material into popular forms; craft narratives and explanations that make scholarly work accessible to the general public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain an institutional publicity office
rubrics_metrics.description: Colleges and universities should maintain a publicity office with a director and staff 'for the purpose of establishing friendly relations with the newspapers, and through the newspapers, with the public.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional leaders should institutionalize publicity functions (appoint secretaries/directors of information) to manage relations with media and the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leadership responsibility for institutional image
rubrics_metrics.description: It is part of the president's work to see that his university takes its proper place in the community and therefore also in the community mind; to produce the results desired culturally and financially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Senior leaders must diagnose whether negative impressions stem from media misrepresentation or institutional shortcomings and act—either by adjusting PR or by modifying institutional programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnose and act on public impressions
rubrics_metrics.description: If the public is getting an oblique impression, the impression should be modified; or if the impression is correct, the work of the university itself should be modified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public relations counsel must determine whether to change public perception through publicity or to recommend substantive institutional changes to align reality with desired image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct or emphasize institutional facts strategically
rubrics_metrics.description: If an institution is mistakenly seen as 80% postgraduate research, 'If it is false, it should be corrected by high-spotting undergraduate activities. If, on the other hand, it is true...the most should be made of that fact.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either highlight activities that counter misperceptions or magnify the factual strengths of the institution through publicity, depending on which approach best serves institutional aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lend experts to public service for publicity value
rubrics_metrics.description: Many universities lend faculty to assist in investigations of public interest (e.g., Cornell lent Professor Wilcox to the national census; Irving Fisher advised on currency matters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facilitate public-facing expert involvement in civic projects—this raises institutional profile and demonstrates public relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect ethical limits and avoid artificial values
rubrics_metrics.description: Propaganda 'may be abused. It may be used to overadvertise an institution and to create in the public mind artificial values.' There is no absolute guarantee against misuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid deceptive overpromotion; strive for accuracy and avoid manufacturing false prestige or misleading claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic choice of event location and spokespeople
rubrics_metrics.description: For causes affecting the entire country, hold events in locations that lend authority to the point of view (e.g., NAACP advised to hold its convention in the South so a southern point of view would carry greater authority); surround events with leaders and local authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select venues and invite participants whose locality and reputation increase the event's persuasive authority among target audiences; recruit both national and relevant local leaders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assemble diverse and locally credible coalitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Support of leaders of diversified groups and group leaders of the region (including local ministers who supported interracial amity) was sought to emphasize the conference's purposes to the entire public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create coalitions that combine national prominence with local credibility to broaden acceptance and make ideas discussable across constituencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize events with symbolic contrasts and spotlights
rubrics_metrics.description: The program used dramatic elements and spotlighted symbolic pairings (e.g., a national leader agreeing with a Baptist preacher from the South) to attract attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use theatrical or symbolic elements and contrasting personalities to create memorable images and generate press interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use press coverage and editorials to amplify impact
rubrics_metrics.description: The event was created with component parts to awaken interest and 'The editorials in the southern press...showed that the subject had become one of interest' because of participation by southern leaders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design events so they are newsworthy to local and national editors; leverage editorial response to shift public discourse and measure influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow up with targeted communications
rubrics_metrics.description: Further publicity was attained by mailing reports, letters, and other propaganda to selected groups of the public after the event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After public events, use targeted mailings and direct communications to selected audiences to sustain momentum and convert attention into support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design social campaigns to change specific habits
rubrics_metrics.description: Social-service campaigns (e.g., to preserve teeth, improve parks, fight tuberculosis, lower infant mortality) are attempts to alter people's habits or opinions through propaganda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define concrete behavioral objectives and craft messages and channels aimed at changing habits; integrate education with persuasive techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use publicity to achieve governmental/administrative reform
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative improvements (e.g., penology in Pennsylvania) are hampered by politics; 'the solution of prison problems...seems to be fundamentally a problem of conscientious and scientific publicity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop enlightened public opinion through systematic publicity to persuade legislatures and administrative bodies to adopt scientific or progressive reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Museums and galleries must interpret and project art
rubrics_metrics.description: Museums 'have little vital relation to life' and 'need to be interpreted to the public'; their function is not merely to receive visitors but to project itself and what it stands for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Museums should dramatize collections, offer lectures, story hours, loan prints, collaborate with commercial firms for applied art, and proactively bring art to communities (e.g., through outreach and usable design).

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish institutional advisory councils to shape taste
rubrics_metrics.description: A museum might establish a museum council of art or a research board for applied arts to set standards in home decoration, architecture, and commercial production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create advisory bodies that translate museum expertise into actionable standards and community-facing programs to raise public aesthetic standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use associational values and recognized authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Public must be interested 'by means of associational values and dramatic incidents.' Example: American silk gained standing by association with Paris and a recognized artist (Edgar Brandt).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Associate products or ideas with recognized authorities, institutions, or cultural centers to confer credibility and desirability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborate with commerce to raise public taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Applied and commercial art: industry collaborating with artists can inject beautiful motifs into articles of common use and thereby improve public taste and markets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partner artists with manufacturers and retailers to create attractive mass-produced goods that educate public taste and create new markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select media according to shifting relative value
rubrics_metrics.description: The relative value of instruments of propaganda (public meetings, newspapers, radio, motion pictures) is constantly changing; the propagandist must take advantage of shifts the instant they occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuously monitor audience habits and new channels; prioritize media that maximize reach and resonance at the time (e.g., newspapers as primary, but be alert to radio and film).

rubrics_metrics.name: Create events with news value to reach newspapers
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers publish material based on 'news value'—the propagandist must 'breathe the breath of life into an idea' and create events that will compete for editorial attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design publicity so it constitutes news (timely, interesting, important); editors will decide publication on news merit, so craft hooks and timeliness accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose source and present facts accurately
rubrics_metrics.description: The source of the news offered to the editor should always be clearly stated and the facts accurately presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be transparent about origins of information and ensure factual accuracy to maintain credibility and avoid editorial rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match content to magazine editorial policy and audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Magazines 'select material deliberately, in accordance with a continuous policy' and often act as propagandist organs for particular ideas (health, fashion, home decoration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place content tailored to a magazine's theme and audience; supply serialized features or expert articles that fit the publication's ongoing policy and interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use lectures for repercussion, not only attendance
rubrics_metrics.description: The lecture's importance for propaganda lies in its repercussion to the general public (broadcasts, newspaper reports), not merely the number of attendees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange for lectures to be broadcast or widely reported; design events to generate secondary media coverage and broader public discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate and adapt to radio and broadcast business changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Radio may compete with newspapers as an advertising medium; future systems (licensing, who pays) are uncertain, but the propagandist must be prepared to meet and utilize these conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan radio and broadcast strategies proactively, consider integrated air-and-print campaigns, and be flexible to changes in funding and regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize motion pictures as mass carriers that reflect vogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Motion pictures are 'the greatest unconscious carrier of propaganda' and 'can standardize the ideas and habits of a nation'—they usually reflect and emphasize broad popular tendencies rather than stimulate new ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use film for broad diffusion and to reinforce mainstream themes; understand film's market-driven constraints and design messaging that aligns with prevailing tastes for greater acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate and manage personalities carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: A public personality can be dramatized yet overexposed; the public demands a personality to typify a corporation. Once a public figure decides his ends, 'he must regard himself objectively and present an outward picture...consistent with his real character and his aims.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct public images consistent with real character and objectives; avoid manufacturing personas inconsistent with private conduct; treat personalities as strategic assets to be managed like other facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer educational material only if accurate and meritorious
rubrics_metrics.description: If a corporation contributes materials to a school to show how a product is made, 'these propaganda activities, if they are accurate and candid, are in no way reprehensible...provided the school authorities accept or reject such offers carefully on their educational merits.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When placing educational content in schools or institutions, ensure accuracy, candor, and educational value; respect institutional gatekeeping and standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use all available avenues and be alert to new means
rubrics_metrics.description: There are a multitude of avenues of approach to the public mind (schools, television, pictures, parades, personal appearances); the propagandist must be alert to make use of all means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate multi-channel campaigns, experiment with emerging media, and be adaptive—combine direct events, mass media, and targeted outreach for cumulative effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt sophistication of methods to public awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: If the public becomes more intelligent about publicity methods, 'its leaders will present their appeals more intelligently'—but basic appeals remain effective because public needs (food, amusement, beauty, leadership) persist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuously raise the sophistication of messaging and tactics as publics become more media-literate, while still addressing fundamental human interests and needs.
